title: Development of Force Concept
lead: Kinematics describes how an object moves and says nothing about why it moves that way. Dynamics asks the second question, and it begins with force. This section gives a working definition of force as a push or a pull with both a magnitude and a direction, shows how the forces acting on a body add as vectors and how a free-body diagram draws only the forces that reach the body from outside, and takes the restoring force of a stretched spring as a standard that any other force can be measured against.
summary_html:
• Dynamics is the study of how forces affect the motion of objects.
  • Force is a push or pull that can be defined in terms of various standards, and it is a vector having both magnitude and direction.
  • External forces are any outside forces that act on a body. A free-body diagram is a drawing of all external forces acting on a body.
notes: The AP item on the direction of the net force on two cars driving around a racetrack is set with Newton’s second law in 4.3, where the net external force is introduced, and its three drawings go there with it.

figures.original_caption: Part (a) shows an overhead view of two ice skaters pushing on a third. Forces are vectors and add like other vectors, so the total force on the third skater is in the direction shown. In part (b), we see a free-body diagram representing the forces acting on the third skater.

The force exerted by a stretched spring can be used as a standard unit of force. (a) This spring has a length x when undistorted. (b) When stretched a distance Δx, the spring exerts a restoring force, F_restore, which is reproducible. (c) A spring scale is one device that uses a spring to measure force. The force F_restore is exerted on whatever is attached to the hook. Here F_restore has a magnitude of 6 units in the force standard being employed.

exercises.prompt: A hawk accelerates as it glides in the air. Does the force causing the acceleration come from the hawk itself? Explain.

answer.solution: A body cannot exert a force on itself. The hawk may accelerate as a result of several forces. The hawk may accelerate toward Earth as a result of the force due to gravity. The hawk may accelerate as a result of the additional force exerted on it by wind. The hawk may accelerate as a result of orienting its body to create less air resistance, thus increasing the net force forward.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following is an example of a body exerting a force on itself?
  1. a person standing up from a seated position
  2. a car accelerating while driving
  3. both of the above
  4. none of the above

answer.solution: A force is a push or a pull that one body exerts on another, and only the external forces, the ones that reach a body from outside it, affect its motion. A body therefore cannot exert a force on itself. A person standing up pushes down on the floor with their legs, and it is the floor pushing back up on the person that raises them; a car accelerating turns its wheels against the road, and it is the road pushing forward on the tires that carries the car along. In each case the force that changes the motion comes from outside the body, so neither the person nor the car is exerting a force on itself and the last of the four options is the one to choose.

exercises.prompt:
What causes the force that moves a boat forward when someone rows it?
  1. The force is caused by the rower’s arms.
  2. The force is caused by an interaction between the oars and gravity.
  3. The force is caused by an interaction between the oars and the water the boat is traveling in.
  4. The force is caused by friction.

answer.solution: Only a force that reaches the boat from outside it can drive the boat forward, so the thing to look for is what outside the boat the oars press against. The rower and the oars travel with the boat and are part of the same body, and a body cannot exert a force on itself, so the rower’s arms are not the answer. Gravity pulls straight down on the boat rather than along the water, and friction with the water opposes the motion rather than causing it. What is left is the water itself: the blades of the oars press backward against the water, and the force the water exerts on the oars in return is external to the boat and points forward. The interaction between the oars and the water is what moves the boat, which is the third of the four options.

exercises.prompt: Propose a force standard different from the example of a stretched spring discussed in the text. Your standard must be capable of producing the same force repeatedly.

answer.solution: Any arrangement will serve as a standard provided it can be set up again and again and produce the same force every time, which is the one property the text asks of a standard. One possibility is to hang a particular metal cylinder from a string at a fixed place on the Earth: the downward pull it exerts on the string is the same each time the cylinder is hung there, and the pull of two such cylinders is twice the standard, so any other force can be stated as a multiple of it. Another is to stretch a fixed number of identical rubber bands by a fixed distance, which is the arrangement of the Take-Home Experiment in this section. A third is the magnetic force between two wires a fixed distance apart carrying a fixed current, which is the standard the text says we will meet in Magnetism. In each case the point is the same: the force can be reproduced at will, so it can be counted.

exercises.prompt: What properties do forces have that allow us to classify them as vectors?

answer.solution: A force has both a magnitude and a direction, and both matter. A cannon exerts a strong force on a cannonball, while Earth exerts only a tiny downward pull on a flea, and in each case the direction of the push or the pull says as much about what happens as its size does. Having a magnitude and a direction is what makes a quantity a vector, and it is why a force can be drawn as an arrow whose length is its magnitude and whose direction is the direction of the push. Forces also combine the way vectors combine rather than the way ordinary numbers do: when two skaters push on a third in different directions, the two pushes add head to tail and the total force points somewhere between them, with a magnitude that is less than the sum of the two magnitudes unless the pushes happen to point the same way. Because they have magnitude and direction and add head to tail, forces can be handled with the same graphical and trigonometric methods that were developed for vectors in Two-Dimensional Kinematics.
